messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Martin Keller, a 50-year-old psychologist in private practice, had spent most of his adult life relying on language. He was used to helping other people find words for fear, shame, and grief, and he had long understood himself as steady, thoughtful, and capable under pressure. The assault fractured that sense of himself in a way he still struggled to describe. Several months before seeking help, he had attended a professional gathering at a hotel bar after a training. He remembered the sharp smell of liquor on another man’s breath and clothing when the man followed him into a quieter corridor and then into a room. After that, Martin’s account thinned into fragments of bodily terror and humiliation. What remained most powerfully was not a coherent visual sequence but the sense of being handled, overpowered, and used. Even now, when he tried to tell the story, he would stop abruptly, his jaw tightening, as if he were pushing the memory away before it could fully form. He would say that he could feel the event in his body with full force, yet could not seem to put what happened into words.

In the weeks afterward, he returned to work and tried to continue seeing patients, telling himself that maintaining his schedule would prove he was still himself. Instead, ordinary moments in his office building began to undo him. If a patient came in carrying the faint smell of alcohol, or if sirens rose from the street below during session, he felt an immediate wave of discomfort that seemed out of proportion to what was happening around him. In those moments, what frightened him most was not only the surge itself but what it seemed to say about him. He had come to believe that he was no longer capable of doing the things that had defined him, that whatever had happened in that hotel had reduced him from a person with agency to an object something could be done to. The smell of alcohol or the cry of sirens did not just unsettle him; they seemed to confirm his bleakest conclusions that he was damaged, deadened, less than fully human now.

Those beliefs hardened quietly over time. Martin described feeling dead inside with his wife and in his office, as if some essential animating part of him had gone out. He increasingly judged every flinch, every unsettled moment, as evidence that the assault had permanently altered him. Holding that view made it harder for him to approach the memory directly. Whenever he sensed the event nearing consciousness, he cut it off before it was complete, almost reflexively, as though allowing the whole thing into words would seal the fact that he had become only an object in his own mind. He could sit with the emotional intensity of the assault—shame, dread, a sickening helplessness—without any clear image at all, and his inability to narrate it only deepened his conviction that he was no longer capable in the way he had once been.

The more inaccessible the memory felt, the more Martin took that as proof of damage rather than as a symptom of trauma. He noticed that when the event came back as a wordless flood—terror without pictures, bodily distress without a story—he felt especially stripped of personhood. Not being able to tell it, not being able to hold the memory from beginning to end, left him certain that the assault had erased something fundamental in him. Each failed attempt to recall it fully seemed to verify his sense that he was dead inside and had lost the abilities that once defined both his work and his identity.

By then, his fear had sharpened his attention to the world around him. Because he already believed he was irrevocably changed and vulnerable, he moved through his day scanning for anything that might signal another collapse: the stale scent of alcohol in the hallway outside his practice, a distant siren passing during an afternoon session, even the first subtle feeling of being uncomfortable in his own body. His appraisals made these cues loom larger and arrive faster. In his office, he began cracking a window in winter to clear the air, shortening sessions when city noise was heavy, and bracing himself before opening the waiting-room door. He understood the irony that, as a psychologist, he could recognize trauma responses in the abstract, yet from the inside it felt simpler and more damning: these reactions meant he was no longer who he had been.

At home, his wife experienced him as present but unreachable. He was not describing new conflicts so much as an absence; he sat beside her at dinner and felt hollow, unable to explain why a passing ambulance outside could leave him mute for the rest of the evening. What finally brought him to treatment was a recent session in which a patient mentioned meeting friends at a bar. Martin caught the smell of alcohol from the man’s coat, felt the now-familiar jolt of discomfort, and lost his train of thought entirely. For the first time in his career, he worried in the moment that he could not do his job. Seeking help felt humiliating, but also necessary. He said he was afraid that if this continued, the assault would define him more completely than his own life had. What he wanted, cautiously and without much confidence, was to feel like a person again and to be able to face what happened without disappearing from himself.
